title: Valued Within Exercises
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: The sixth Will to Learn strategy, Valued Within Exercises are designed so that students, not the teacher, generate their own reasons for valuing coursework. Stuart offers four concrete formats: a monthly utility-value t-chart intervention, Why Conversations in which students respond to a hypothetical skeptic ranting that the subject is pointless, a recurring find our class in the world homework assignment, and end-of-unit Pop-Up Debates prompting students to name the most interesting concept from the unit. Each example is built so students think their way into Value rather than simply receiving the teacher's argument for why the work matters.
points: The defining feature across all four examples is that students, not the teacher, generate the reasons for valuing coursework, thinking their way into Value rather than being told.
The Why Conversations format stages a hypothetical outsider ranting that the subject is pointless, then has students respond via quickwrite, Think-Pair-Share, or Pop-Up Debate.
A colleague's weekly mathy moment homework assignment builds social pressure over time, so that within a month students roll their eyes at a peer who claims they couldn't find one.
End-of-unit Pop-Up Debates asking students to name the most interesting concept double as content review, public speaking practice, and a Valued Within exercise simultaneously.
quotes: It's any exercise that gets students thinking about why their coursework matters (Valued) to them (Within).
The key in looking at these examples is to notice that, in each case, students are being given the task of determining why the work matters. They are thinking their way into Value.
Pose a scenario to your students in which a person from the street walks into the classroom and starts ranting about how your class is pointless.
Within a month or so, students in class will roll their eyes when one of their peers says, I couldn't find one. They'll say things like, C'mon, did you have to be anywhere on time?
I like to use prompts like this for end-of-unit Pop-Up Debates. It helps with content review, public speaking practice, student engagement…and with Valued Within.
